To answer your question, no. I'm not a stickler for rules in general but I do feel that table manners are something to be observed in polite society. I'm not so much referring to the examples that you've mentioned, I'm thinking more along the lines of not putting elbows on the table, speaking with food in one's mouth or using a phone at the dinner table. To me, it's a common courtesy to adhere to basic table manners.

I think table manners still matter as much as our parents' generation, but we define "table manners" differently. So, it's sort of a yes-and-no response. What they considered proper etiquette has evolved and now we have our own perceptions of proper etiquette.

Take, for instance, the value of the nuclear family. That was probably more ingrained into the minds of people who lived in an era in which the husband was the head of the household and breadwinner, while the wife was expected to be the homemaker, and the children subservient. This would tie into the father sitting at the head of the table, with the wife opposite him, and the children sitting on the broad sides of the table. Nowadays, there is more of a diversity in types of families, so that etiquette has been phased out. As technology has progressed, new things have become important to our generation. For instance, turn off or silent your mobile device, and refrain from text messaging. These types of manners were completely non-existent during my parents' generation.

To put it simply: table manners reflect societal values, and values are always changing.

Photo by Neal Ulevich awarded a 1977 Pulitzer Prize for Spot News Photography.

The Thammasat University Massacre was an attack on students and protesters that occurred on the campus of Thammasat University in Bangkok, Thailand by right wing students and national police. Left wing students from various universities were demonstrating against the return to Thailand of former military dictator Field Marshal Thanom Kittikachorn. By the official count, forty-six people died in the attack, during which protesters were shot, beaten and their bodies mutilated.

The left-wing students eventually surrendered. As photographer Ulevich was heading towards the University gates "I saw some commotion in the trees. I walked down there and I saw a body hanging. He was certainly dead, but the crowd was so enraged that a man was hitting the body on the head with a folding chair. I stood there to see if anybody was looking at me. Nobody was. I took a few frames and walked away."

A junta headed by the defense minister, Admiral Sa-ngad Chaloryu, seized power immediately after the massacre. The membership of the junta was more moderate than that of Pramarn's faction and the relationship between the factions remains poorly understood. The junta installed Tanin Kraivixien, a hard-line anti-communist and a royal favorite, as prime minister.
